'''Park Jong-sei''' (born 1943), also spelled '''Park Jong-se''', is a South Korean chemistry researcher and former government official. He rose to worldwide notice during the [[1988 Summer Olympics]] in Seoul for his role in detecting [[Ben Johnson (Canadian sprinter)|Ben Johnson]]'s steroid use. He was later the head of South Korea's Food and Drug Administration (now the [[Ministry of Food and Drug Safety]]) under President [[Kim Dae-jung]] from March 1998 until January 1999, and founded [[protein microarray]] development start-up Lab Frontier in 2002.

==Early career==
A graduate of [[Seoul National University]]'s Department of Chemistry, Park moved to the United States to earn a PhD from [[Johns Hopkins University]] and then did [[postdoctoral research]] at [[Georgetown University]] before joining the faculty of Georgetown and the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Maass |first=Peter |date=1988-12-10 |title=SEOUL DRUG TESTING HAD ITS SURPRISES |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1988/12/10/seoul-drug-testing-had-its-surprises/4c2bb014-359c-4fe0-b015-43994a200bc7/ |access-date=2022-04-02 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref> He later naturalised as a U.S. citizen and worked for the [[government of Maryland]]'s Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Park moved back to South Korea in 1986, where he served as head of the [[Korea Institute of Science and Technology]]'s Applied Sciences Division. He resumed his original South Korean citizenship and [[relinquishment of United States nationality|relinquished U.S. citizenship]] in 1996 before joining the Food and Drug Administration, as South Korea did not permit [[multiple nationality|dual citizenship]] at the time.<ref name="Yonhap19980308">{{cite news|url=http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&sid1=102&oid=001&aid=0004377799|author=Chae Sam-seok [蔡三錫]|title=朴鍾世 식품의약품안전청장|trans-title=Park Jong-sei, Food and Drug Administration chairman|work=[[Yonhap News Agency]]|date=1998-03-08|accessdate=2014-02-08}}</ref>

In his capacity at KIST, Park was involved with [[drug test]]ing at the [[1988 Summer Olympics]] in Seoul as head of the Olympic Doping Control Center.<ref name="MoneyToday20020218">{{cite news|url=http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&sid1=101&oid=008&aid=0000141690|title=박종세 전 식약청장, 벤처사장 변신|trans-title=Former FDA head Park Jong-sei transforms into start-up president|work=[[Money Today]]|date=2002-02-18|accessdate=2014-02-10}}</ref> There, he was responsible for the detection of [[stanozolol]] in urine and blood samples from [[Ben Johnson (Canadian sprinter)|Ben Johnson]] which resulted in the latter being stripped of his gold medal. Park took great care in performing the [[urinalysis]], and even repeated the test procedure from scratch to be entirely sure of his results before reporting the sample to International Olympic Committee officials; he did not find out to whom the sample belonged until days later, as the [[Blind experiment|samples were not labelled by name]] per standard procedure.<ref name="Yonhap19980308"/><ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1067804/3/index.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121106124119/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1067804/3/index.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=6 November 2012|first1=William Oscar|last1=Johnson|first2=Kenny|last2=Moore|title=The Loser|magazine=Sports Illustrated|date=1988-10-03|accessdate=2014-02-10}}</ref> ''[[ABC World News]]'' named him "Person of the Week" on 30 September 1998 for his role in bringing the scandal to light.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://tvnews.vanderbilt.edu/program.pl?ID=118247|first=Peter|last=Jennings|authorlink=Peter Jennings|title=Person of The Week (Jong-Sei Park)|work=ABC Evening News|date=30 September 1998|accessdate=2014-02-10}}</ref> He also detected marijuana usage by three athletes, though no action was taken against them as marijuana was not a banned [[performance-enhancing drugs|performance-enhancing substance]]. Park clashed with Olympics officials over other aspects of how he did his job, and made angry comments to the ''[[Washington Post]]'' about false samples with trace amounts of banned substances which had been planted among genuine samples in his lab.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-12-11-sp-486-story.html|title=Planted Samples Upset Seoul Drug-Test Chief|work=Los Angeles Times|date=1988-12-11|access-date=2014-02-10}}</ref> His work at the Olympic Doping Control Center earned him the [[Scientist of the Year Award]] by the Korea Science Journalists Association.

==As head of the Food and Drug Administration==
Park was appointed head of the Food and Drug Administration in March 1998.<ref name="Yonhap19980308"/> His appointment came as a surprise to observers, as he was a scientist in what was typically viewed as a political position. In his new capacity, he conducted a shake-up of the administration, replacing seven long-serving officers and recruiting more than 40 new scientists from South Korea and overseas. Park's disregard for earlier seniority-based promotion procedures elicited opposition from the bureaucracy, and the ''Chosun Ilbo'' reported that some disgruntled anti-reformists in the administration had made anonymous denunciations to prosecutors about Park's alleged receipt of bribes, resulting in an investigation of him just months after he was appointed to his new position.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://english.chosun.com/site/data/html_dir/1998/08/13/1998081361475.html|author=Lim Ho-joon|title=Reporters' Notes: Undaunted Reformist|work=[[The Chosun Ilbo]]|date=1998-08-13|accessdate=2014-02-10}}</ref>

In January 1999, Park was arrested on bribery charges, with prosecutors stating that for several years beginning in 1992, a local pharmaceutical company executive had paid him ₩185 million in bribes for his aid in getting the company's drugs approved. Park's arrest was part of President [[Kim Dae-jung]]'s crackdown on corruption in the medical industry, and was followed in February by the arrest of Park's director-general of pharmaceutical safety Kim Yon-pan.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Joanne|last=McManus|title=South Korea cracks down on medical corruption|journal=British Medical Journal|volume=318|issue=7185|page=692|date=13 March 1999|pmc=1115147|pmid=10074010|doi=10.1136/bmj.318.7185.692b}}</ref> Park was convicted on the charges and sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation.<ref name="Bosa20071129">{{cite news|url=https://www.bosa.co.kr/umap/nzine_view.asp?nzine_PK=121&page=212|author=Yoon Young-jin|title=20 months after BE fabrication cases, Park Jong-se arrested|work=Bosa Magazine|date=2007-11-29|accessdate=2014-02-08}}</ref> He served roughly two years of his sentence, and was released in 2000.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&sid1=101&oid=081&aid=0000087395|title=박종세 초대 식약청장 연루|work=[[Seoul Shinmun]]|date=2006-04-26|accessdate=2014-02-10}}</ref>

==Later career==
In 2002, Park founded Lab Frontier, a biotechnology start-up which collaborated with [[Ewha Womans University]] on [[protein microarray]] development.<ref name="MoneyToday20020218"/> He also later became president of the Bio Venture Association.<ref name="Bosa20071129"/> In November 2007, he was arrested on fraud charges relating to alleged falsification of pharmaceuticals trial reports used to get regulatory approval for pharmaceuticals, on the basis of a tip from a paid informant which led to indictments of 22 other researchers.<ref name="Bosa20071129"/><ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&sid1=100&oid=001&aid=0002423817|title='약효시험 조작' 신고자에 5천만원 포상|trans-title='Pharmaceuticals trial fabrication' informant gets ₩50 million reward|work=[[Yonhap News Agency]]|date=2008-12-23|accessdate=2014-02-10}}</ref>
